content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making several changes to the App Store in an effort to increase the platform's revenue potential.

The specific changes Apple plans to make to the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman notes that Apple wants to "find ways to improve margins and squeeze more recurring revenue from the platform," and that this effort is being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current SVP of Services Eddy Cue.

According to reports, this plan is one of the reasons senior Apple employee Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller stepped down as SVP of Marketing in 2020 and was named an Apple Fellow, with one of his responsibilities including oversight of the App Store. Schiller was not in favor of the ideas described above:

Apple has a number of potential ways to improve App Store margins. One of them would be eliminating the human app review process; in an era of agentic coding, this process is costly and not necessarily effective. However, further automating the review process could upset users, even though it would indeed save money.

Hot takes from SF:

Given that Apple is one of the most valuable companies in the world, if this is true, it's a really bad and completely unnecessary move, and a really bad signal from the incoming CEO. I was hoping that having someone with a hardware background take over would help Apple refocus on products rather than services, but engaging in this kind of activity just seems greedy. I hope it's not true.

Apple could raise the developer membership fee, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 per month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, Apple could theoretically raise the fee further without too much pushback. Apple could also charge large developers per-traffic subscription fees to share some of the infrastructure costs.

What the final result will be remains to be seen, but I'm very interested to see what form these changes ultimately take.
